content:
TL;DR #Training Small LLMs from Scratch: Lessons from Zagreus and Nesso introduces two families of openly released sub-billion-parameter language models for Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and French, together with the full recipe used to build them. This is a collaboration with the MiiLLM project.
Problem #Small Language Models are attractive for consumer hardware, edge devices and privacy-sensitive applications, but most open efforts focus on English and a few high-resource languages. Romance languages have few openly available models trained from scratch, and few transparent, reproducible baselines.
What did we do? #We trained Zagreus, four bilingual foundation models pairing English with Italian, Spanish, Portuguese and French. Each has about 400 million parameters and was trained from scratch on roughly one trillion tokens. Nesso extends these models with supervised fine-tuning for instruction following and agentic function calling, including a fully open variant trained only on public data. The paper describes the whole pipeline: data curation, tokenizer design, architecture, distributed pre-training, post-training and evaluation.
Main findings #Carefully curated data and transparent training practices let sub-billion-parameter models stay competitive with larger baselines of comparable class. Nesso-0.4B-instruct matches or exceeds Qwen3-0.6B on several Italian and English benchmarks, and Zagreus-0.4B-por outperforms Qwen3-0.6B-Base on the Portuguese leaderboard. Structured prediction and discriminative classification remain targets for future data augmentation and alignment work.
Resources # Read the paper Models on Hugging Face Cite this paper #@inproceedings{ercolani2026zagreus, title = {Training Small LLMs from Scratch: Lessons from Zagreus and Nesso}, author = {Ercolani, Alessandro and Federici, Edoardo and Bentivogli, Luisa and Corbucci, Luca}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the Twelfth Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics (CLiC-it 2026)}, year = {2026} }
title: Training Small LLMs from Scratch: Lessons from Zagreus and Nesso

content:
TL;DR #FeDa4Fair: Client-Level Federated Datasets for Fairness Evaluation introduces a benchmark and a library for studying fairness in Federated Learning when clients have different and potentially conflicting biases.
Problem #When training Federated Learning models, we usually evaluate fairness with metrics aggregated across the whole federation. These global scores can hide the individual clients. A model may appear fair overall while treating some clients much worse than others because of their data distributions, sensitive attributes, or fairness requirements differ.
What did we do? #We created FeDa4Fair, a collection of benchmark datasets designed for client-level fairness evaluation. The datasets model heterogeneous client populations and make it possible to compare fairness-aware Federated-Learning methods under controlled and reproducible conditions. The clients considered in the benchmark datasets may have attribute-level or value-level conflicting preferences.
Moreover, we also introduce a library that allows to easily create datasets with certain unfairness distributions simulating both attribute- and value-level conflicting unfairness.
Resources # Read the paper FeDa4Fair datasets on Hugging Face Code and documentation Cite this paper #@inbook{10.1145/3805689.3812291, author = {Heilmann, Xenia and Corbucci, Luca and Cerrato, Mattia and Monreale, Anna}, title = {FeDa4Fair: Client-Level Federated Datasets for Fairness Evaluation}, year = {2026}, isbn = {9798400725968}, publisher = {Association for Computing Machinery}, address = {New York, NY, USA}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1145/3805689.3812291}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency}, pages = {2462–2501}, numpages = {40} } }
title: FeDa4Fair: Client-Level Federated Datasets for Fairness Evaluation

content:
TL;DR #Rashomon Sets and Model Multiplicity in Federated Learning studies what happens when several Federated models perform almost equally well in terms of privacy but differently in terms of other metrics such as fairness.
Problem #Federated Learning usually produces one global model by averaging updates from many clients. That model can hide important differences between clients: a model that performs well on average may still fail on a particular client or group of clients. In centralized Machine Learning, the collection of similarly accurate but behaviorally different models is known as a Rashomon set. In this paper we studied how to define and study those sets without collecting clients’ raw data in the Federated Learning setting.
What did we do? #We formalized three federated perspectives:
Global Rashomon set: models that satisfy a performance constraint across aggregated client data. t-agreement Rashomon set: models that satisfy the constraint for a chosen fraction of clients. Individual Rashomon set: models that each client considers sufficiently accurate for its own data. We also designed a privacy-compatible pipeline for generating candidate models. The pipeline requires at most two additional communication rounds beyond standard training.
Main findings #Experiments on Dutch Census, ACS Income, and MNIST show that global evaluation can hide large differences in local model behavior. Increasing the client-agreement threshold makes the set smaller and filters out models that only perform well on average. Individual clients can also observe multiplicity patterns that are very different from global averages.
Resources # Published Paper 📓 Code 🧑🏻‍💻 Cite this paper #@inbook{10.1145/3805689.3812290, author = {Heilmann, Xenia and Corbucci, Luca and Cerrato, Mattia}, title = {Rashomon Sets and Model Multiplicity in Federated Learning}, year = {2026}, isbn = {9798400725968}, publisher = {Association for Computing Machinery}, address = {New York, NY, USA}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1145/3805689.3812290}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the 2026 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency}, pages = {2434–2461}, numpages = {28} }
title: Rashomon Sets and Model Multiplicity in Federated Learning

content:
These are some notes I took while learning about Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture. Most of the content is based on the lecture 3 of the Stanford CME295 course on Transformers and LLMs, but I also added some information from other resources. I also discussed about this topic in my podcast, it is in Italian.
Introduction #Mixture of Experts (MoE) is an architecture that aims to increase the model performance while keeping the inference cost low. This architecture has been used in some recent LLMs such as Mixtral, Qwen and Deepseek but it is now also used in a lot of other models.
Differently from the standard Transformer, you take the original Feed-Forward layer (FFN) and replace it with a sparse version consisting of multiple expert copies. Behind these copies there is a router that selects which of these experts to use for each token in each forward pass at inference time.
Benefits of MoE #LLMs are huge in terms of number of parameters, this requires a lot of time for both training and inference. The initial idea was to have bigger and bigger models to increase their capabilities. Later a smarter approach, Mixture of Expert (MoE), has been introduced.
MoE allows the model to increase the number of parameters contained in the model, consequently decreasing the loss. At the same time, obviously, this requires more memory to store the parameters. However, the key idea behind MoE is that you can increase the parameters of your models by 10x while limiting the increase in FLOPs. If you have a classic dense model and you increase the number of parameters by 10x, you’ll need to do more computation for each token you process. Instead, with MoE, you can have 10x more parameters but only activate a fraction of them for each token you process. This means having a bigger model while keeping the training cost of a smaller one.
At inference time you have a similar benefit, only a subset of these parameters will be used for each token, keeping the inference cost low. In terms of FLOPS, the MoE model allows to have more parameters per FLOPS compared to a dense model.
Let’s consider Mixtral 8x7B, if you think about the number of parameters, it could be 8*7B = 56B. In reality, the number is lower, 46.7B, because while the FFN layers are multiplied by 8, the rest of the model is shared. Considering what we have said before about the model activations, during the model inference only 2 of the 8 experts are activated. This means that in total, the parameters used for each token are 12.9B, which is the same as a 12B dense model.
Note that even if the number of activate parameters is 12.9B, we still need to load all the parameters 46.7B parameters in the GPU memory.
The other benefit we can have with MoE is the parallelization that we can obtain, each expert can be stored in a different device or GPU. The router will then be responsible for getting the token and activate the correct expert on the correct device. This means that if we have a continuous stream of input data, the different devices can be kept busy and we can have a high throughput. On the contrary, if we have a single device, it might make more sense to directly use a dense model instead of a MoE one, because the cost of loading all the parameters in memory could be higher than the cost of using a smaller dense model.
Where are the experts located? # Let’s consider the image above, we have a part of the transformer architecture. Specifically, we are interested in the Feed-Forward layer (FFN). This layer has an amount of parameters that is \( d*d_{ff} + bias \) where \( d \) is the dimension of the input and is O(hundreds) while \( d_{ff} \) is the dimension of the hidden layer and is O(10K). Because of this amount of parameters, the FFN is the best place where to put the MoE architecture. When using MoE you typically replace the FFN with a MoE version of it, where you have trained multiple FFNs and route every token to a different FFN. The router takes the representation of the token and figures out which expert is the best for that token.
Mixture of Experts Architecture #Given the input \( x \), you ask who should get activated for that input and then you only activate those experts. This is the idea behind Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture. To do this, not only you need some experts but you also need a gate (or router) that tells you which expert should be involved.
flowchart LR X[X] G[G] %% Junction nodes representing the arrows intersecting J1((x)) J2((x)) J3((x)) E1[E1] E2[E2] E3[E3] %% The output node using LaTeX formatting Y("$$\hat{y}$$") %% X goes up to G X --> G %% X goes through the junctions to the Experts X --- J1 --> E1 X --- J2 --> E2 X --- J3 --> E3 %% G drops down into the pathways (junctions) G -.-> J1 G -.-> J2 G -.-> J3 %% Experts merge to output E1 --> Y E2 --> Y E3 --> Y %% Optional styling to make junctions look like small operation points style J1 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px style J2 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px style J3 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:1px Let’s consider the example in the image above. The gate, we have the input x, the gate G and three experts. The output \( \hat{y} \) can be computed as follows: $$\hat{y} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} g_i(x) \cdot E_i(x)$$
Based on the value that \( g_i(x)$ takes, we can have two different scenarios:
If \( g_i(x) \) is a binary value, then we have a Sparse MoE. In this case, only the top-k experts will be activated (k is an hyperparameter that we can set) and only a part of the system will be run. If the \( g_i(x) = 0 \) then the corresponding expert won’t be activated. This first solution is used to lower the amount of flops required for inference. If instead \( g_i(x) \) is a continuous value between 0 and 1, then we have a Dense MoE. In this case, we do not have a constraint on the number of experts that can be activated. Some weights will be higher than others but all the parameters will be used for all the inputs. The router \( G \) can be a simple network with a softmax function: $$G(x) = \text{Softmax}(Wx + b)$$ that will give us a probability distribution over the experts.
Inference time # flowchart LR subgraph Inference Time direction LR X[X] --> MMHA["Masked Multi
Head Attention"] MMHA --> G[G] %% Gate routing to experts G -- "prob distr
(choose top k)" --> FF1["FFN_1"] G -- "prob distr
(choose top k)" --> FF2["FFN_2"] G -- "prob distr
(choose top k)" --> FF3["FFN_3"] end At inference time, the input x is passed to the Masked Multi-Head Attention (MMHA) and then to the gate G. Even if we have multiple attention heads, the gate is shared across all of them because their inputs are concatenated and projected. The gate then, computes for each token the probability distribution over the experts and selects the top-k experts to activate.
Challenges #When building LLMs with MoE architecture, we have to face some challenges:
Routing collapse: some experts can be more popular than others and can be selected more often by the router while others are never involved in the computation. To mitigate this, a change in the loss can be introduced to force other experts to be selected. $$\mathcal{L} = \alpha \cdot N \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{N} f_i \cdot P_i$$
Where \( P_i \) is the average probability of selecting the expert \( i \) while \( f_i \) is the fraction of tokens that are routed to expert \( i \).
The key idea behind MoE is that you can increase the parameters of your models while limiting the cost at inference time because you only activate a part of them. The number of experts that you can have is an hyperparameter and is independent of the attention heads. The choice of the expert can be different in the different layers, for instance, we can route token i in layer 1 to expert 1 and in layer 2 to expert 3. The router is layer specific and is trained together with the rest of the model.
Useful resources # Stanford CME295 Transformers & LLMs | Autumn 2025 | Lecture 3 - Tranformers & Large Language Models Mixtral of experts Mixture of Experts Explained
title: Notes on Mixture of Experts

content:
TL;DR #Interpreting Federated Learning by Aggregating SHAP Explanations introduces iFLASH, a framework for producing global explanations from local SHAP explainers without centralizing client data.
Problem #Federated learning keeps training data on local clients, but conventional explainability methods often assume centralized access to that data. Simply averaging local explanations can also be misleading when clients have different data distributions or model quality.
What we did #In iFLASH, clients compute and evaluate SHAP explanations locally. Instead of sharing raw data, models, or gradients, clients send feature-importance information and performance-based quality measures to the server. The server then uses aggregation strategies that weight client contributions according to model performance and explanation quality.
We evaluate the framework in both cross-silo settings with a small number of clients and cross-device settings with many clients, including heterogeneous data distributions.
Main findings #Quality-aware aggregation improves explanation faithfulness over naive uniform averaging in cross-silo experiments. The resulting explanations align closely with centralized explanations in feature-importance ranking and directionality. In cross-device settings, quality-aware methods remain competitive as the larger number of clients creates a stronger averaging effect.
Resources # Read the paper Cite this paper #@article{bonsignori2026iflash, title = {Interpreting Federated Learning by Aggregating SHAP Explanations}, author = {Bonsignori, Valerio and Corbucci, Luca and Naretto, Francesca and Guidotti, Riccardo and Monreale, Anna}, journal = {IEEE Access}, year = {2026}, doi = {10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3696009} }
title: Interpreting Federated Learning by Aggregating SHAP Explanations

content:
It’s the end of the year again, but this one feels different. I’m not in my hometown with my family. Instead, I’m in the city where I currently live, because of one of the problems that shaped much of my 2025. This was not the best year of my life. Together with my partner, we had to face several personal challenges, and I also had to deal with a health issue that forced me to slow down and take time off. Still, despite everything, we made it to the end of the year, and we’re finally getting close to what I’d call a normal life again.
Some reflections on 2025 #Looking back, I can roughly split 2025 into three parts.
The first one was short but intense: from January to FOSDEM 2025. During those weeks I worked extremely hard to finish two papers and submit one to FAccT 2025. That paper was later accepted, and I consider it one of the biggest achievements of this year—and of my PhD as a whole.
The second part, from February to October, was by far the hardest. We were dealing with multiple personal problems, and at the same time my back issues started to get worse. I had to stay at home, see a surgeon, and wait for a call for surgery. Despite everything, during this period I still managed to complete several projects, submit them to different conferences, and finally submit my PhD thesis. Some of those works were accepted, some were not, but we’re still working on them.
The last part of the year, from October to December, was the recovery. I had the surgery and started the rehabilitation process. It wasn’t easy, but I’m now slowly starting to feel better.
My feelings about 2025 are mixed. On one side, I’m genuinely happy about some major achievements, including the defense of my PhD. On the other, I feel a sense of sadness for the time lost to health issues and personal struggles.
Defending my PhD also marked the end of my journey at the University of Pisa. It closed a long chapter of my life that began in 2014, when I moved to Pisa to start my Bachelor’s degree. Over more than a decade, that city gave me experiences, friendships, and memories that I’ll always remember. Eventually, though, I felt it was time to move on and start a new adventure.
Right now, the future is still uncertain. I’m looking for new opportunities and asking myself many questions. Do I want to continue as a researcher? Do I want to move to industry? I don’t have clear answers yet, but I’m sure the new year will bring some clarity.
Some photos from 2025 #There are a few highlights from 2025 that I really want to remember:
January, the submission to FAccT 2025 of a paper, which was then accepted. February – FOSDEM 2025. FOSDEM means meeting friends, having fun in Brussels, eating fries, and drinking beer. I won’t be there this year, and I’ll miss it a lot.
London! We went there for the Flower Summit 2025. I had the chance to present a poster and to finally visit the city. I’ll never forget this, especially because when I came back home my problems at my back worsened a lot. FAccT 2025 in Greece! The defense of my PhD thesis. The surgery and the beginning of the recovery. I don’t have many plans or goals for 2026. I just want to fully recover from my surgery, find a job that makes me happy, and, one year from now, look back with gratitude for what 2026 brought, while staying close to the people I love the most.
title: 2025: Year in Review

content:
Installing and setting up Immich on macOS and Android should be a straightforward process. However, I faced so many issues during the installation and setup that I want to share here the steps I followed to make everything work.
Installing Immich on MacOS using Docker #Initially, I tried to install Immich using Docker following the tutorial on the official documentation. However, the PostgreSQL container was not working correctly, and it was failing with the error “initdb: error: could not change permissions of directory “/var/lib/postgresql/data”: Operation not permitted”. I tried to change the permissions of the folder, but it was not working. After some search, I found someone in a thread on AnswerOverflow having exactly the same issue. In the comments, I also found the solution:
It may seem strange, but I had to go to this page and read what was written in the “Special requirements for Windows users” section to solve the problem. Apparently, the Immich Postgres database must be located on a filesystem that supports user/group ownership and permissions (EXT2/3/4, ZFS, APFS, BTRFS, XFS, etc.). The solution is to change the bind mount to a Docker volume. Therefore, in the .env file, I had to change:
- DB_DATA_LOCATION=./postgres + DB_DATA_LOCATION=pgdata And in the docker-compose.yml file, I had to add:
volumes: model-cache: + pgdata: After this small change, I was able to restart again the containers and everything worked fine.
Android Setup #I installed the Immich Android app from the Play Store, and I had two main issues during the setup. First of all, it did not want to connect to the server. I was using Tailscale to connect my Mac Mini and my Android phone to the same network. However, the app was not able to connect to the server using the Tailscale IP address. After some research, I found that Android has an additional setting for the VPN hidden inside the settings of each VPN. Specifically, you have to enable the “Always-on VPN” option. This will allow the Immich app to connect to the server using the Tailscale IP address.
The second issue instead was related to the background upload of the photos. I noticed that even if the phone was connected to WiFi and charging, the app was not uploading the photos in the background. Again, I had to search a bit and make some tests to find the solution. Even in this case, the solution was hidden inside the Android settings. I activated the “Allow Background usage” option, but this was not enough.
Then, I discovered that clicking on the “Allow Background usage” option opens a new page in the Android settings where you have to enable the “Unrestricted data usage” option for the Immich app.
I have to admit that coming from the iOS world, all these options, not only hidden inside the settings but even difficult to find, are a bit confusing. However, after enabling these two options, the Immich app was able to upload the photos in the background without any issues.
title: Installing and setting up Immich on MacOS and Android

content:
TL;DR #An Interpretable Data-Driven Unsupervised Approach for the Prevention of Forgotten Items introduces methods for reminding shoppers about products they may have intended to buy but omitted.
Problem #Shopping-recommendation systems often focus on suggesting new products. A different and practical problem is predicting a forgotten item: a product a person is likely to need or buy regularly but did not include in the current basket.
What did we do? #We formalized forgotten-item prediction as an unsupervised learning problem. The proposed methods, XMT and TXMT, combine signals such as purchase recurrence, time between purchases, seasonality, co-purchases, and sequential shopping patterns.
The approach is designed to remain interpretable. Instead of returning only a score, it can expose the behavioral signals that support a reminder, such as a product’s usual purchase interval or its relationship with the current basket.
Main findings #The experiments compare the proposed methods with next-basket and forgotten-item baselines on real retail data. The data-driven models improve prediction quality while retaining human-readable reasons for their recommendations.
Resources # Read the paper Cite this paper #@inproceedings{corbucci2025forgotten, title = {An Interpretable Data-Driven Unsupervised Approach for the Prevention of Forgotten Items}, author = {Corbucci, Luca and Borges Legrottaglie, Javier Alejandro and Spinnato, Francesco and Monreale, Anna and Guidotti, Riccardo}, booktitle = {Proceedings of the 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence}, year = {2025}, doi = {10.3233/FAIA250912} }
title: An Interpretable Data-Driven Unsupervised Approach for the Prevention of Forgotten Items

content:
Some time ago, in the Superhero Valley Discord server, one of our users asked whether going to tech conferences could be helpful for a student and what conferences to attend. I answered the question with my opinion on this topic, and then I thought it could be a good idea to write a post about it.
My first tech event #My history with tech events started more than 15 years ago (yeah, I feel old while thinking about this). It was 2008 when my mother told me that she had seen an advertisement about an event called “Linux Day” organized by a local community called Tulug. At that time, I did not even know what Linux was, but I was already extremely attracted to computers. I shared this event with a classmate and we decided to go together. I still remember that day, it was a Saturday afternoon, and after school we went to the Linux Day.
As it happens, in most of the tech events we had the opportunity to attend some talks, but most importantly, we received as a “gift” some CDs with a Linux distribution and a lot of stickers. I still have those CDs and stickers in a box in my room in my parents’ home. That day, I discovered a new world, and I started to be more and more interested in computers and technology. The chat I had with the organizers was so interesting for a 13-year-old child, and watching people working with Linux distributions with a lot of passion was something that I will never forget. I have to admit that at that time, I was particularly attracted by the effects that all of the organizers were able to have on their PC with Linux. This was probably the reason why that day, I decided that I had to try Linux.
Unfortunately, as far as I know, the Linux Day was organized only a few times in my city, and I was only able to attend it three times. Therefore, these three events were the only tech events that I attended until the beginning of University, more than 5 years later.
Attending the events from the last row #In 2014, I started my Computer Science degree in Pisa. Just after a few months, in May 2015, some people organized a watch party for the Google I/O. Since I was used to watching these kinds of events alone at home, I found this a nice thing and I decided to attend the event with some of my friends. I don’t remember too much of that day except for the fact that a room with ~150 seats was almost full of people interested in the event. That one was the first event of the GDP Pisa. Starting from that day, for the following 4 years, I attended almost all of the events organized by this community and a few other events organized by another local community called Gulp. The biggest mistake I made while taking part in these events was to attend them “from the last row”. I was interested in the talks, but I used to avoid the networking part as much as I could. I was not used to taking part in the beer party after the events or talking with people that I did not know. My biggest mistake was to think that the people who were organizing these events were too “important” and distant from me, so that I could not have the confidence to spend time with them in front of a beer after the event.
The Erasmus #The turning point in my experience with tech meetup was the Erasmus. I moved to Munich to spend a semester abroad in October 2019. My main goal was to improve my English, which was terrible at that point. Despite following lectures in English and spending time with other students, I felt that this was not enough and that I was not challenging myself enough to improve my English. By chance, I found an advertisement for an event organized by the DSC Munich and I decided to attend it. It was only the first of dozens of events that I attended in Munich during the 5 months I was there. A key event was when I started to attend the Flutter Munich meetup. They organized a Hackathon, and then I started to attend their meetup. It was mind-blowing for me. I had never used Flutter before, but I started to attend all the events and talk with all the other attendees. I think I never expressed enough my gratitude to the organizers of the Flutter Munich meetup. It was really important for me, and in the next section I’ll explain why.
Changing perspective #After attending the Flutter meetups, I started to learn Flutter and to work with it. I remember that when I was close to the end of my Erasmus, in one of the last meetups I attended, I asked the organizers for some tips on how to organize a Flutter Meetup when I was back in Pisa. They gave me some suggestions, and then I went back to Italy with the idea that I wanted to organize a Flutter Meetup in Pisa. It was the end of February 2020. I guess you all know what happened in March.
I have never organized a Flutter Meetup in Pisa, but after just a few months, my friends and I started something bigger. Thanks to a series of lucky events, we had the opportunity to interact with a Googler who proposed that we gather a group of students interested in preparing for tech interviews all together.
That was the start of Superhero Valley.
Superhero Valley’s goal is to fill the gap between the Italian universities and the Big Tech Companies. Initially, we decided to organize some talks to raise awareness of the opportunities offered by Big Tech companies. At the same time, we started to do LeetCode exercises together. In just a few months, we went from a local community open only to the Computer Science master students of Pisa University to an online community with more than 1000 members coming from all around Italy. The growth of Superhero Valley continued during the next years, and today we have more than 2200 members in our Discord server. Our activities also changed over time. We introduced a new mentorship program that allowed us to pair a mentor with one or more mentees who could guide them in their professional growth. We did our best to track the results of the community, measuring the number of ‘active’ members (mentees, people who joined the exercise group) that received an offer for an internship or for a full-time position in Big Tech. We have more than 100 people who received an offer.
Later, in 2022, Antonio proposed to launch a local startup in Pisa, thought of by computer scientists and tech enthusiasts. We started this community in July 2022. Our first event was a big success.
After that one, we organized a lot of other events in Pisa, and we even had the opportunity to host meetups with international speakers. Organizing local meetups was something new to me. My previous organizational experience was with online meetups. Organizing and hosting a local meetup is something completely different, and I liked it a lot from the first time. The biggest difference that pushes me to continue organizing in-person meetups is mainly what happens after the event: the pizza (or beer) party. During the after-party, you have the opportunity to talk with a lot of interesting people, and this is something that you usually cannot do when organizing an online event.
Giving back something to the community #Besides the effort that I’ve put in during these years to lead communities and organize events, I also wear another cap as a volunteer. This happened multiple times for the organization of the DevFest Pisa and at the Fosdem AI DevRoom in 2025.
Why should you be a volunteer at a conference for a day instead of spending a relaxing day listening to talks and talking with people?
In my case, the answer lies in the idea of giving back something to the community. I started to feel the “urge” to be a volunteer when I recognized how these communities had on me during the time. Being a volunteer and helping them prepare the welcome kit for participants, introducing speakers before their talk, or just checking in participants is an easy way to give them back something, helping them deliver the best possible event for all the attendees.
Conclusions and suggestions #Attending community events and meetups is something that has shaped me a lot over the years. I would not be the person I am today without the exposure to these events and, most importantly, to the people in the communities.
At this point, it could be easy for me to just recommend that you find a community you might like, try to attend their meetups, and then, if you feel it, try to be involved in the organization. However, I want to conclude the article with a few bullet points to clarify some things that I think are crucial:
I believe that each of us has to find a reason when joining a community. Being involved in the community can be rewarding, but it can also be demanding; you must have the right motivation to do that. You should not do that just to put yourself in a “power” position or for your personal goal. Remember that the most important thing is the healthiness of the community, of the organizing team, and the value you give to the people who will attend your event. Kill your ego: You must be open to being the last one to join, being open to learn new things about how a community works. Be honest with yourself: Regarding the effort needed to join a community, it is essential to be honest with themself, don’t overestimate the time you can dedicate to the community. It is better to do just a few things than promise that you’ll do a lot and then disappear without saying anything.
title: From last row attendee to community organizer

content:
TL;DR #Enhancing Local Explanations with GAN-Based Neighborhood Generation presents FIRE360, a local and model-agnostic explanation method for tabular machine-learning models.
Problem #Local explainers need a neighborhood of examples around the instance being explained. If that neighborhood is generated poorly, the explanation can contain unrealistic samples and become difficult to trust. Standard perturbation strategies may also struggle with mixed or structured tabular data.
What did we do? #FIRE360 uses a generative adversarial network to create a reusable synthetic neighborhood around the data distribution. It then provides several complementary views of a model decision:
Feature-importance information; Factual and counterfactual rules; Representative exemplars; Counter-exemplars showing how nearby decisions differ. The method is model-agnostic and is intended to provide more than a single ranking of features.
Main findings #FIRE360 combines feature importance, factual and counterfactual rules, and representative examples so that an explanation can show both why a prediction was made and how it could change.

title: Enhancing Local Explanations with GAN-Based Neighborhood Generation

content:
TL;DR #A Benchmark for Client-Level Fairness in Federated Learning proposes a benchmark for measuring whether fairness improvements in a federated model benefit individual clients.
Problem #Federated learning combines data from many clients without moving their raw records to a central server. This creates a tension in evaluation: global metrics are easy to report, but they can hide poor outcomes for particular clients.
What did we do? #We propose a client-level benchmarking framework that compares global fairness with fairness measured separately for each client. The benchmark considers heterogeneous client datasets and differences in sensitive-attribute distributions, making it possible to test whether an algorithm is robust to realistic client variation.
The evaluation can be used to compare federated-learning methods, fairness metrics, and mitigation strategies under the same experimental setup.
Main findings #A single federation-wide score is not enough to understand fairness. Reporting client-level results reveals when a method improves the average while leaving some clients behind.

title: A Benchmark for Client-Level Fairness in Federated Learning

content:
TL;DR #Differentially Private FastSHAP for Federated Learning Model Explainability combines federated learning, model explanations, and differential privacy.
Problem #Explainability methods often require access to training data or synthetic samples. In federated learning, sharing those data can violate the privacy assumptions that motivated federation in the first place. Explanations therefore need their own privacy-aware training process.
What did we do? #We adapt FastSHAP to a federated setting and add sample-level differential privacy during the training of the explainer. Clients contribute to the explanation model without sharing their raw data. The resulting system can produce feature-attribution explanations for a collaboratively trained model while limiting information leakage from the explanation process.
Main findings #Model explanations should be treated as a potential privacy channel. Adding differential privacy to the federated explainer makes it possible to study the utility–privacy trade-off rather than assuming that explanations are automatically safe.

title: Differentially Private FastSHAP for Federated Learning Model Explainability

content:
TL;DR #Benefits of the Federation? Analyzing the Impact of Fair Federated Learning at the Client Level asks whether joining a fair federated system benefits every client, rather than only improving a global metric.
Problem #Federated learning brings together clients with different data distributions and potentially different fairness requirements. A fairness intervention that helps the federation overall may still reduce utility or fairness for a particular client.
What did we do? #We studied the client-level effects of fair federated learning and compared methods including FedMinMax, PUFFLE, and reweighting strategies. The experiments evaluate both global outcomes and the performance and fairness experienced by individual clients.
Main findings #Global fairness improvements do not automatically translate into benefits for every client. The results show that client heterogeneity can create trade-offs: a method can improve an aggregate objective while leaving some clients with worse local outcomes.

content:
TL;DR #PUFFLE: Balancing Privacy, Utility, and Fairness in Federated Learning introduces a method for studying the trade-offs between privacy protection, model utility, and fairness while training Federated Learning models.
Problem #Federated learning keeps data local, but model updates can still reveal information. Differential privacy can reduce that risk, yet adding noise may lower accuracy or affect groups differently. Optimizing privacy and utility alone can therefore create new fairness problems.
What did we do? #PUFFLE incorporates privacy, utility, and fairness into the federated-learning objective. The method uses tunable parameters to control the relative importance of these goals and evaluates how the trade-offs change across different client distributions.
Main findings #There is no single setting that is optimal for every federation. The right balance depends on the privacy budget, the data distribution, and the fairness objective. Making those choices explicit helps practitioners understand the consequences of a deployment.
Resources # Read the paper Preprint on arXiv Cite this paper #@inproceedings{corbucci2024puffle, title = {PUFFLE: Balancing Privacy, Utility, and Fairness in Federated Learning}, author = {Corbucci, Luca and Heikkilä, Mikko A. and Solans Noguero, David and Monreale, Anna and Kourtellis, Nicolas}, booktitle = {ECAI 2024}, year = {2024}, volume = {392}, doi = {10.3233/FAIA240671} }
title: PUFFLE: Balancing Privacy, Utility, and Fairness in Federated Learning

content:
TL;DR #Enhancing Privacy and Utility in Federated Learning: A Hybrid P2P and Server-Based Approach with Differential Privacy Protection explores a federated architecture that combines peer-to-peer communication with server-based aggregation.
Problem #The central server in a traditional federated-learning system simplifies coordination but can become a privacy and scalability bottleneck. Differential privacy can protect updates, but the additional noise may reduce model utility.
What did we do? #We designed a hybrid architecture in which clients can exchange information through peer-to-peer connections while retaining server-based coordination where it is useful. We also studied how differential-privacy protection affects model performance in this setting.
The experiments compare privacy and utility under different configurations and analyze how the architecture changes the cost of privacy protection.
Main findings #Federated learning does not have to rely on a single communication pattern. Combining peer-to-peer and server-based mechanisms can offer another point in the design space for balancing privacy, communication, and model utility.
Resources # Read the paper Cite this paper #@conference{corbucci2024hybrid, author={Luca Corbucci and Anna Monreale and Roberto Pellungrini}, title={Enhancing Privacy and Utility in Federated Learning: A Hybrid P2P and Server-Based Approach with Differential Privacy Protection}, booktitle={Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Security and Cryptography - Volume 1: SECRYPT}, year={2024}, pages={592-602}, publisher={SciTePress}, organization={INSTICC}, doi={10.5220/0012863600003767}, isbn={978-989-758-709-2}} }
title: Enhancing Privacy and Utility in Federated Learning: A Hybrid P2P and Server-Based Approach with Differential Privacy Protection

content:
TL;DR #Semantic Enrichment of Explanations of AI Models for Healthcare connects Machine Learning explanations with the clinical language used by clinicians.
Problem #Feature-importance explanations can identify which variables influenced a prediction, but they do not always provide enough context for a clinician. In healthcare, the relevant evidence may be expressed in clinical notes using concepts and terminology that are not directly represented by the model features.
What did we do? #We enriched explanations using medical ontologies, including SNOMED CT, and natural-language processing of clinical notes. The method links features that contribute to a prediction with semantically related information in the patient’s notes.
Main findings #Adding clinical semantics can make model explanations more informative than a list of feature names or scores. It helps connect a model’s internal evidence with concepts that healthcare experts already use.

title: Semantic Enrichment of Explanations of AI Models for Healthcare

content:
TL;DR #Explaining Black-Boxes in Federated Learning adapts feature-attribution explanations to models trained collaboratively across multiple clients.
Problem #Federated learning protects data locality, but this makes it difficult to apply centralized explainability methods. A server cannot simply collect all client data to explain the global model, and explanations produced independently by different clients may not be directly comparable.
What did we do? #We designed a method that computes local explanations at the clients and combines the resulting feature attributions to explain predictions from the federated model. The approach builds on SHAP-style explanations while keeping the data on the clients.
Main findings #A federated model can be explained without centralizing the records used to train it. Aggregating local attribution information provides a global view while preserving the distributed nature of the learning process.

content:
I’ve spent part of this afternoon trying to install Tensorflow on my M1 Mac. I tried to install it writing “tensorflow” in the requirements.txt file but it didn’t work and I always had the following error:
ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement TensorFlow (from versions: none) Then I’ve found out that I needed to use a different tensorflow version so I’ve put “tensorflow-macos” and “tensorflow-metal” in the requirements.txt file.
Unfortunately, I had another error, this time related to “hdf5”:
ERROR: Could not build wheels for h5py which use PEP 517 and cannot be installed directly In the end, I was able to solve this error with the following commands:
brew install hdf5 pyenv exec pip install --no-binary=h5py h5py Then I finally installed “tensorflow-macos” and “tensorflow-metal”.
Note tha sometimes it is possibile to do the same thing with other packages (for example I’ve tried with box2d-py).
title: How to install hdf5 on M1 Mac

Laptop Setup #With the beginnning of my postdoc, I started using a Dell . I haven’t been used anything different than macos in the last 10 years and at the beginning it was a bit of a shock to go back using a Linux distribution. Choosing which Linux distribution to use was easy, I wanted to have 1) something that could work out-of-the-box without too much work on customization 2) a distro with a tiling window (I was used to use Aerospace on MacOS and cannot live without it anymore). I decided to give a try to Omarchy because I’ve heard a lot of discussion about it and I was curios. I started using it in March 2026 and now (August 2026) I’m still using it. I recently updated it to version “Quattro” and I relly like this distro.
Desktop Setup #Ergonomicity ^^^^^**** # My desk is a Rodulf Standing Desk by Ikea, a cheap standing desk that I bought in 2021. It’s big enough and I can’t live without it now. I’ve tried many desk lamps over the past few years. All of them have something that I did not like. In the end, I tried the Xiaomi Mi Computer Monitor Light Bar and I think that it’s the best compromise between space occupied on the desk and light produced. Keychron K8 - This has been my main keyboard for some years, now I use it mainly connected to the Dell Laptop. Rode NT-USB - This is the microphone I use for recording podcasts. Software for macOS # Hidden Bar Aerospace is a porting of i3 to macOS. I’ve never used something like this in the past but after I started using the Samsung Odyssey G9 I decided to try it to exploit as much as possible the space offered by this monitor. Alfred Espanso is an open-source text expander developed by Federico Terzi. Federico was a guest in a PointerPodcast episode. Amphetamine I use Bitwarden as my password manager. Even if the user experience could be improved, I like their culture a lot. It is Open source and with the free version, you would be able to use it without too many limitations. Notion Fantastical Tailscale Other stuffs I use # iPad 11th generation with A16 chip - I use it mainly for reading, taking notes and watching videos.
